title: US Memories reborn: take-or-pay consortium with escrowed exit penalties
idea: US Memories (1989; IBM, DEC, HP, Intel and others) collapsed before breaking ground because members walked away when DRAM prices fell. Fix exactly that: members sign 10-year take-or-pay offtake contracts for capacity units (wafer starts per month) with a price collar, and post exit penalties equal to their share of unrecovered capex into escrow, so a price dip cannot dissolve the fab.
why: Capital intensity and U.S. manufacturability: pre-selling ~60-70% of output cuts the cost of capital for a $15B+ fab by several points and keeps a U.S. DRAM fab financeable through a downturn.

title: Qimonda lesson: counter-cyclical strategic DRAM wafer reserve
idea: Qimonda went bankrupt in the 2008-09 crash with buried-wordline technology in hand because no one would bridge a 12-month cash trough. Fix: a sovereign reserve buys finished DRAM wafers and known-good dies at a cost-based floor during busts, stores them in nitrogen cabinets (unpackaged wafers keep for years), and releases them at a ceiling price during shortages like 2026.
why: Keeps capacity alive through troughs and flattens spikes: a reserve of ~5% of annual bits could hold a 4x spike nearer 2x, and it prevents capacity destruction that takes $15B and 4 years to rebuild.

title: Richmond fab clause: reversionary option keeps closed fabs warm
idea: When Qimonda's 300 mm fab near Richmond, Virginia closed in 2009, its tools were sold off and the U.S. lost a DRAM fab for good. Fix: every subsidized fab carries a reversionary option, so on closure the government can buy the cleanroom, utilities and tools at depreciated book value, keep them at minimum burn (purge, utilities, skeleton crew), and lease them to a new operator.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital: restarting a warm shell takes ~12-18 months and ~30% of greenfield capex, versus 3-5 years and $15B+ for a new fab.

title: Elpida's yen-and-cycle death: a cleared DRAM bit futures market
idea: Elpida failed in 2012 with competitive technology, killed by a strong yen and a price cycle it could not hedge. Fix: a cleared futures and options exchange on a standard contract (e.g. 1 Tb of DDR5-equivalent per quarter, cash-settled against a published contract-price index) lets makers sell forward and buyers lock in supply, as airlines hedge jet fuel.
why: Capital intensity: hedgeable revenue could cut memory makers' risk premium by ~2-3 points of WACC, worth ~$300-450M a year on a $15B fab, and buyers' forward commitments fund new capacity earlier.

title: Anti-RDRAM: royalty-free open DRAM macro kit for any foundry
idea: Rambus RDRAM lost the market around 1999-2002 to royalty resentment, licensing litigation and a closed design. Fix the opposite way: a buyer-funded foundation releases an open-source, patent-pledged DRAM design kit (cell layouts, sense amplifiers, refresh controller, PHY, BIST) characterized on several mature foundry processes, so any fab can enter DRAM-class memory without licensing a closed process.
why: Lowers the entry barrier (years of design work and ~$100M+ of IP and litigation exposure), which adds second-source capacity in U.S. and allied fabs.

title: HMC's mistake fixed: open multi-vendor base die for HBM stacks
idea: Micron's Hybrid Memory Cube died as a closed consortium product built on a single-vendor logic base die, and it lost to JEDEC HBM. Fix: standardize the core-die-to-base-die interface (TSV map, protocol, test hooks) so any maker's DRAM core dies can be stacked onto any foundry-made base die, and smaller DRAM makers can sell qualified core dies into HBM.
why: HBM TSV tax and supply concentration: widens the pool of HBM core-die suppliers beyond three firms and moves base-die silicon out of scarce DRAM fabs.

title: OMI done right: generation-agnostic CXL buffer reuses retired DDR4
idea: IBM's OpenCAPI Memory Interface (and FB-DIMM before it) died tied to one CPU vendor and one buffer supplier. Fix: an open CXL Type-3 card whose buffer drives DDR3, DDR4 or DDR5 on its back side, so DIMMs pulled from retired servers go back into new servers behind CXL, with the buffer adding ECC and patrol scrub to manage aged parts.
why: Reuse: hyperscalers retire very large volumes of working DDR4 each year; a second 4-5-year life could add ~20-30% to usable supply at ~10-20% of the cost of new bits.

title: Relabel scandal fixed: certified, graded reclaimed DRAM chips
idea: Harvested DRAM from e-waste got a bad name because chips were sanded, remarked and sold as new. Fix: a certified reclamation line desolders and reballs each chip, runs full retention, speed and row-hammer characterization, writes a tamper-evident provenance record (original lot ID read from the die's fuses plus test results), and sells the chips openly in graded tiers with warranty.
why: Supply: turns millions of discarded DIMMs into trusted bits at a fraction of new cost; recovering even ~5% of annual bit demand matters when prices are 4x.

title: Optane's App Direct trap fixed: transparent tiered memory with SLA
idea: Optane DIMMs disappointed because the best mode (App Direct) needed rewritten software and Memory Mode had poor tail latency. Fix: sell any cheaper tier (dense, slow-bin or NAND-backed memory) only behind a CXL controller that migrates hot 4 KB pages into local DRAM in hardware, priced against a contractual DRAM-equivalent latency SLA, with zero code changes.
why: Lets data centers cut fast DRAM per server by ~30-50% at the same delivered performance, which frees bits for AI.

title: Lehi fab lesson: swing fab toggling new memory and DRAM
idea: 3D XPoint's dedicated Lehi fab ran far below capacity, and its fixed cost helped kill Optane. Fix: launch any new memory in a swing fab whose toolset is ~80% shared with a DRAM flow, with a dual-qualified recipe library, so wafer starts move between DRAM and the new memory each quarter as demand changes.
why: Capital intensity: a new memory rides DRAM's utilization (keeping the fab ~85%+ loaded) instead of carrying an empty fab, and in shortages the same tools make DRAM.

title: Nantero's contamination wall: bolt-on BEOL annex for exotic memory
idea: Nantero's carbon-nanotube NRAM spent more than a decade on adoption because fabs would not let CNTs (or other exotic materials) into their lines. Fix: a small back-end annex beside a logic or DRAM fab receives finished CMOS wafers in sealed pods, deposits and patterns the new memory layers in its own cleanroom, and returns sealed wafers, so the host line never touches the material.
why: Removes the main adoption barrier for new memory materials; an annex costs ~$0.3-1B versus $15B for a fab and lets new memories use existing CMOS capacity.

title: The Machine had no fab: tool-condominium ownership inside fabs
idea: HPE's memristor and The Machine stalled because HPE owned no fab and its manufacturing partner put its own roadmap first. Fix: a fab condominium where memory designers and large buyers own specific tools (e.g. one ALD cluster, one etch bay) inside an operator's fab, depreciate them on their own books, and hold guaranteed slots on those tools.
why: Capital intensity and access: splits a $15B fab into $10-100M tool-sized stakes that hyperscaler capital can buy, and guarantees fab access for new memory technology.

title: Z-RAM retargeted: floating-body bits from underused FD-SOI foundries
idea: Innovative Silicon's Z-RAM died because standalone DRAM makers found the floating-body cell's margin too thin for commodity parts, and the startup had no fab. Fix: target FD-SOI logic foundries (22/28 nm, often underused) that already run SOI wafers, offering a standard macro that uses thin-BOX back-gate bias to widen the sense margin, and build memory chiplets there that bond to processors.
why: Adds DRAM-class bit supply from logic capacity outside the three DRAM makers, with no capacitor module and no EUV.

title: Jinhua's fatal IP taint fixed: escrowed full-process license transfer
idea: Fujian Jinhua's DRAM fab was effectively killed in 2018 by trade-secret charges and an export ban, because the provenance of its process was tainted. Fix: an allied entrant licenses a complete legacy-node DRAM process (recipes, masks, yield database, seconded engineers) from an incumbent, with royalties escrowed against yield milestones and government-backed indemnity.
why: U.S. manufacturability: cuts an entrant's learning curve from ~10 years to ~3 and removes the legal risk that can kill a fab outright.

title: Inmos killed by impatience: statutory 15-year memory charter
idea: Britain's state-backed Inmos (founded 1978) was sold to Thorn EMI in 1984, mid-ramp, when political patience ran out. Fix: a statutory memory charter funded in pre-legislated tranches over 15 years, released on technical milestones (yield, bits shipped) rather than quarterly profit, and run by an independent trust that cannot be sold during the term.
why: Capital intensity and time: DRAM needs 3-5 years to build and ~5 more to learn yield; matching funding to that horizon removes the political cancellation risk that killed earlier national programs.

title: Helium reserve sell-off answered: closed-loop helium recapture per tool
idea: The 1996 Helium Privatization Act sold off the U.S. federal helium reserve, and Qatar's outage now starves fabs. Fix: fit recapture skids to every helium-using tool (backside wafer cooling in etch and implant, purge, leak check) that collect helium from the exhaust, purify it with membranes and pressure-swing adsorption, and feed it back to the tool.
why: Scarce resources: ~80-90% less helium bought per wafer, turning a geopolitical chokepoint into a small top-up.

title: Twin Creeks revived: proton-exfoliated thin DRAM wafers spare crucibles
idea: Twin Creeks' Hyperion proton-implant exfoliation (slicing ~20 um silicon sheets off a thick donor) died in the 2012 solar price crash. Fix: apply it to DRAM by exfoliating many thin device-grade layers from one CZ donor block and bonding each to a cheap recycled or polycrystalline handle wafer, so one crystal ingot yields 10-20x more device wafers.
why: Scarce resources: cuts high-purity quartz crucible and polysilicon use per wafer by roughly 10x, which matters when Spruce Pine supplies >80% of crucible quartz.

title: Mapper's throughput death fixed: e-beam writes only cuts on gratings
idea: Mapper's massively multi-beam e-beam lithography went bankrupt in 2018 because writing whole layers was too slow (~10 wafers per hour). Fix: use multibeam only for the sparse cuts and contact holes on top of self-aligned quadruple-patterned gratings (DRAM arrays are highly periodic), so the beams expose ~1-2% of the area and effective throughput rises ~50x.
why: EUV chokepoint and capital: replaces 2-4 of DRAM's EUV layers with tools costing a fraction of a $200M scanner, ending single-supplier lock-in for those layers.

title: 450 mm died on toolmaker risk: tools paid per wafer pass
idea: The 450 mm transition (G450C) was abandoned around 2016 because toolmakers would not fund development without guaranteed volume. Fix the risk split: toolmakers own and maintain tools inside the fab and are paid per wafer pass with uptime guarantees, so fab capex becomes opex and toolmakers profit from throughput and yield.
why: Capital intensity: depreciation is ~55% of DRAM wafer cost; per-pass pricing could cut an entrant's upfront capital ~50-70% and align toolmakers with uptime.

title: Diablo's litigation death: buyer fund buys orphaned memory patents
idea: Diablo Technologies' Memory1 died after patent litigation drained it, while orphaned portfolios from Qimonda, Elpida, Spansion and others went to patent assertion entities. Fix: a defensive patent fund financed by memory buyers acquires distressed memory portfolios at auction, grants royalty-free licenses to members' suppliers, and offers litigation cover to new entrants.
why: Lowers the legal risk and royalty load that has sunk memory startups, making it cheaper for new DRAM-class suppliers to enter.

title: Audio-RAM for AI: approximate grade from row-failed dies
idea: In the 1990s partly defective DRAMs were sold as audio RAM for answering machines, until flash ended that market. Fix: create a formal approximate grade whose bad-row maps ship in the module's SPD, and use these dies for error-tolerant AI data (activations, low-order KV-cache bits, embeddings), with the framework placing critical data only on clean rows.
why: Yield: recovers perhaps 3-8% of wafer output that is now scrapped or deeply discounted, a large number of bits in a shortage.

title: ScaleMP's software DSM fixed: CXL-switched rack memory pool
idea: ScaleMP's vSMP (software distributed shared memory across servers) faded because network latency made remote pages slow and fragile. Fix: pool memory in hardware with a CXL switch shelf, where each server borrows 1 GB slices at ~250-400 ns under a fabric manager and returns them when jobs end.
why: Usable supply: clouds strand ~25-30% of server DRAM unused; pooling can cut fleet DRAM purchases by ~10-15%.

title: SoftRAM fraud made real: rack-wide content-addressed page deduplication
idea: SoftRAM 95 promised doubled memory and did nothing, and RAM Doubler died as operating systems absorbed it. Fix with a real mechanism: a CXL memory node hashes 4 KB pages from every server in a rack and stores identical pages (OS images, libraries, shared model weights, zero pages) once, mapped copy-on-write back to each host.
why: Cuts physical DRAM ~15-40% in VM and container fleets where pages repeat across hosts, not only within one host.

title: Anamartic Wafer Stack redux: self-configuring wafer-scale memory slabs
idea: Ivor Catt's Anamartic wafer-scale memory (1989) chained good dies on an uncut wafer into a spiral but died because hand-assembled wafer stacks could not keep up with falling DRAM die prices. Fix with 1990s tools only: on fully depreciated 200 mm, 180 nm lines, pattern whole wafers of DRAM tiles with built-in self-test that fuses a spiral chain through good tiles, and ship each wafer as one memory slab with no dicing, die packaging or per-die sort.
why: Capital and U.S. manufacturability: uses zero-book tools in idle 200 mm fabs and removes packaging and test (~25-35% of module cost); ~5-7 GB per 200 mm wafer, so it is surge capacity, not a cost-per-bit leader.

title: MoSys 1T-SRAM afterlife: hidden-refresh DRAM replaces legacy SDRAM
idea: MoSys's 1T-SRAM (DRAM cells with hidden refresh behind an SRAM interface, built at 180 nm for Nintendo's GameCube) faded as embedded memory moved on. Fix: build standalone 64-512 Mb SRAM-interface DRAM chips on 180 nm, 200 mm lines to replace the SDR/DDR/DDR2 parts that industrial, automotive and defense customers still buy and the big makers are retiring.
why: Supply: moves legacy-part demand off advanced DRAM lines, and the SRAM-like interface avoids requalifying controllers in products with decades-long lives.

title: T-RAM moved home: thyristor memory built in power-device fabs
idea: T-RAM's thyristor RAM died at a logic foundry (GlobalFoundries) that could not tune doping well enough to tame the thyristor's turn-on variability. Fix: build the thyristor cells in 200 mm power-semiconductor fabs (0.35-0.18 um, 1990s tools), whose engineers tune multi-junction doping and carrier lifetime (proton or electron irradiation) daily for IGBTs and thyristors.
why: Opens a pool of mature fab capacity that has never made memory, for a capacitor-free cell giving a domestic source of low-density, fast SRAM-replacement bits.

title: IBM MXT rebuilt at 180 nm: cold-page compressing module buffer
idea: IBM's Memory eXpansion Technology (2000) doubled server memory with hardware compression but was dropped for its added latency once DRAM became cheap. Fix: a 180 nm buffer chip on the module compresses only cold pages during idle cycles (base-delta and zero-page codecs small enough for 1990s gate budgets), while hot pages stay uncompressed, so most accesses pay no penalty.
why: ~1.5-2x effective capacity on existing DIMMs; at 4x bit prices, a few-dollar 180 nm chip is cheaper than buying the bits.

title: ESDRAM's chipset snub fixed: SRAM row-cache companion die
idea: Enhanced Memory Systems' ESDRAM and Mitsubishi's cached DRAM put SRAM row caches on DRAM in the 1990s but died because Intel chipsets would not support them. Fix without host changes: a separate 180 nm SRAM die on a CXL-buffered module latches each opened row and serves repeated hits itself, so older reclaimed DDR3/DDR4 dies behave like faster parts and open rows far less often.
why: Reuse and energy: makes aged dies usable in latency-sensitive slots and cuts row activations (row-hammer exposure and ~5.9 pJ/useful-bit overfetch) by ~30-50% on workloads with locality.

title: GaAs memory's cost death revisited: junction-storage DRAM in RF fabs
idea: GaAs memories (Gigabit Logic, Vitesse SRAMs) died on cost against silicon in the late 1980s-90s. But GaAs's intrinsic carrier density is ~10^4x lower than silicon's, so thermal leakage falls by orders of magnitude: a JFET- or HEMT-access junction-storage DRAM cell built on 6-inch RF GaAs lines (0.25-0.5 um, 1990s-class, largely U.S.-based) could hold charge for very long times with almost no refresh.
why: Refresh and U.S. manufacturability: taps a compound-semiconductor fab pool outside DRAM's chokepoints for low-density, near-refresh-free working memory; density and wafer cost are the main risks.

title: nCHIP silicon MCMs revived as 180 nm HBM interposers
idea: Early-1990s silicon-substrate multichip modules (nCHIP and others) died for lack of a product valuable enough to pay for them. HBM is that product: run thin-film silicon interposer and bridge lines (0.4-2 um wiring, Bosch-etched through-silicon vias, a 1994 process) in idle 200 mm, 180 nm-0.5 um fabs to add capacity beside the CoWoS-class packaging bottleneck.
why: Packaging capacity limits HBM output as much as DRAM wafers do; 1990s tools can draw interposer-scale lines, adding U.S. supply at a fraction of advanced-fab capex.

title: Irvine Sensors cubes: edge-wired DRAM stacks without TSVs
idea: Irvine Sensors stacked bare memory dies into edge-wired cubes for military use in the 1990s, and the method never went mainstream. Fix: laminate 8-16 thinned standard DDR dies, route their pads to the cube's side face, and pattern the side wiring with 1990s thick-film lithography, giving high-capacity stacks for CXL and server modules without TSVs.
why: HBM TSV tax: capacity (not bandwidth) stacks avoid TSV area (~3x wafer area per bit) and its 20-30% yield loss, leaving HBM-grade wafers for AI.

title: Qimonda trench resurrected in MEMS DRIE fabs: 100 fF cells
idea: Qimonda's deep-trench DRAM lost because trenches could not shrink below ~50 nm. At 180 nm and above, shrinking does not matter: Bosch deep reactive-ion etch in 200 mm MEMS fabs cuts 100:1 trenches, giving ~100 fF cells (vs ~5 fF today) that hold data ~20x longer for the same leakage.
why: Refresh and supply: long retention allows low-refresh buffer DRAM built in MEMS capacity outside the memory oligopoly; density is low, so it targets refresh-light buffer roles, not bulk bits.

title: Bubble memory's slowness fixed: current-driven domain-wall shift lines
idea: Bubble memory (Intel Magnetics, TI) was killed by slow field-driven bubble motion (~100 kHz) and a separate garnet process. Fix: pattern Co/Pt or CoFeB multilayer nanowires at 250 nm and above with 1990s steppers and HDD-media sputter tools, move domain walls with spin-orbit-torque current pulses (~100+ m/s), and reuse bubble memory's major/minor-loop layout and bad-loop map.
why: A non-volatile, refresh-free warm tier that takes cold pages off DRAM, built on old lines; ~10-100 ns per shift step makes block access practical.

title: Ramtron's PZT exile solved: FeRAM in inkjet piezo-MEMS fabs
idea: Ramtron's PZT ferroelectric RAM stayed niche partly because PZT and Pt/Ir electrodes contaminate CMOS lines, which forced a segregated module. Piezo-MEMS fabs that make inkjet heads and sensors already run PZT/Pt/Ir on 200 mm with 1990s-class tools: put the ferroelectric capacitor module there, on top of 0.35-0.18 um CMOS wafers.
why: Opens a non-DRAM fab pool for refresh-free 1T1C ferroelectric memory to replace legacy DRAM and battery-backed SRAM in industrial and automotive uses, freeing commodity DRAM; PZT endurance (~10^12-10^15) is the limit.

title: 2021 PMIC choke fixed: domestic old-node lines for DIMM companions
idea: DDR5 module output was throttled in 2021-22 by a shortage of power-management ICs, and Japan's Minimal Fab (half-inch wafers) struggled for lack of a killer product. Fix: dedicate small domestic 200 mm and Minimal-Fab-style lines (0.18-0.5 um BCD, 1990s-class) to the simple chips every module needs (PMIC, SPD hub, temperature sensor), with buyer-funded buffer inventory.
why: Supply resilience: a $2 chip should never block a $500 module; this removes a chokepoint that has already limited DDR5 module output.

title: Wafer-level burn-in revived with 1990s-made full-wafer contactors
idea: Full-wafer DRAM burn-in (tried in the 1990s-2000s, e.g. Aehr's WaferPak) stalled because full-wafer contactors were costly. Make the contactors with 1990s tools: MEMS spring-probe arrays and polyimide flex membranes patterned at 1-5 um on old 200 mm lines, so every HBM core-die wafer is burned in and screened before stacking.
why: HBM yield is down 20-30% partly because weak dies get stacked; wafer-level screening raises stack yield and relieves test-floor capacity, a bottleneck alongside TSVs.

title: CCD memory reborn in idle sensor fabs for weight streaming
idea: CCD shift-register memory (Fairchild, Intel, 1970s) lost to DRAM because of serial access, and CCD sensor fabs are idling as CMOS image sensors won. Serial access is now a feature: AI inference streams weights and KV blocks in fixed order, so many parallel CCD loops built on 0.35-0.18 um CCD lines can stream blocks at full rate with no row decoders and little periphery.
why: Density and periphery: CCD storage is ~4F^2 with almost no periphery (vs ~49% of a DRAM die), giving a cheap streaming tier from stranded fabs; random access stays poor.

title: ETA10's cryo bet revisited: LN2-cooled legacy-node memory pools
idea: ETA Systems' liquid-nitrogen-cooled CMOS supercomputer (ETA10) died in 1989 from cost and timing, not physics. Fix with cryo for memory only: 180 nm DRAM dies at 77 K leak orders of magnitude less (refresh nearly disappears) and switch ~1.5-2x faster, so pooled LN2-cooled shelves of old-node memory approach modern latency and idle power.
why: Makes depreciated-fab memory performance-competitive (refresh cost near zero, faster transistors); density stays low and cooling overhead is the risk, so it suits pooled capacity tiers.

title: TRRespass fixed off-die: exact hammer counters on 180 nm chip
idea: In-DRAM Target Row Refresh was broken in 2020 (TRRespass) because its small sampler could not track enough aggressor rows. Fix: a 180 nm companion chip on the module keeps exact per-row-group activation counts (Misra-Gries tables in SRAM) and issues neighbor refreshes, so dies that flip at ~1k activations, now down-binned or scrapped, can be sold safely.
why: Row hammer and yield: recovers hammer-weak dies as standard parts and protects scaled DRAM without spending advanced-die area on counters.

title: Printed-memory failures fixed: oxide-TFT DRAM on retired LCD lines
idea: Printed and plastic memories (Thin Film Electronics, Kovio) died without a dense, fast product. Fix: use retired Gen-2 to Gen-4 LCD lines (1990s tools, 1.5-3 um lithography, sputter tools reused for oxide channels) to make 1T1C DRAM in oxide TFTs on glass, where very low off-current gives minutes of retention, over square meters instead of wafers.
why: Capital and U.S. manufacturability: ~2 GB per m^2 on fully depreciated panel tools, so cost per bit rests on cheap area rather than litho; a refresh-light bulk tier at ~100 ns-1 us.

title: Fab fire-sales stopped: strategic bank for 180 nm-plus tools
idea: When Qimonda and other fabs closed, their mature tools went abroad for cents on the dollar, and most retiring 200 mm tools are still exported. Fix: a federal strategic tool bank buys retiring steppers, etchers, furnaces and implanters (180 nm and above), refurbishes them, and leases them cheaply to domestic micro-fabs making memory companion chips, interposers and test hardware.
why: Capital intensity and U.S. manufacturability: 1990s-class tools cost ~1-5% of new, and a standing pool can equip dozens of small U.S. lines.

title: Fab-starved memory startups: 180 nm memory-device MPW shuttle
idea: Memory startups (Unity Semiconductor, Spin Memory, Crossbar and others) spent much of their capital just getting wafers made. Fix: a MOSIS-style multi-project wafer service on a 180 nm, 200 mm line with open back-end memory-module slots (capacitor, ferroelectric, resistive, molecular layers), where startups pay per die site and share masks, getting silicon in ~8 weeks for ~$20k.
why: Cuts the cost of a new memory concept's first silicon ~100x and speeds iteration, raising the odds that a new DRAM-class cell reaches volume.

title: FB-DIMM's hot buffer fixed: off-path refresh-brain rescues weak dies
idea: FB-DIMM's advanced memory buffer died of heat (several watts) because it sat in the data path. Fix: keep a 180 nm buffer off the data path and use it only for control: it profiles each row's retention at boot and drives multi-rate refresh (RAIDR-style), refreshing strong rows rarely and weak rows often.
why: Refresh: cuts refresh energy and bandwidth loss by ~50-75%, and lets dies rejected for a few short-retention rows ship as standard parts.

title: Tera MTA's latency tolerance puts slow 180 nm memory to work
idea: Tera Computer's MTA (1990s) hid memory latency with 128 hardware threads per processor and no data caches, but lost the market. Fix: pair latency-tolerant multithreaded accelerators with memory built on 180 nm lines (~150-300 ns access), so slow but buildable bits do throughput work (graph analytics, sparse math, retrieval) without slowing it.
why: Usable supply: depreciated-fab memory becomes productive capacity, leaving fast DRAM for latency-critical jobs.

title: Back to polycide: tungsten-free legacy-node memory flow
idea: Polycide (WSi, CoSi2) wordlines were abandoned for tungsten because their resistance scaled badly in narrow lines, which now ties DRAM to tungsten (China ~80%). At 180 nm and above that problem does not exist: run legacy-node memory and companion chips with poly/CoSi2 wordlines, Al-Cu interconnect and Ti/TiN-lined Al-reflow plugs (a 1990s technique) instead of W plugs.
why: Scarce resources: removes tungsten from the old-node memory and companion-chip flow, shielding that supply from a single-country chokepoint.

title: ZettaCore's molecules applied last: multi-bit redox cells on 180 nm
idea: ZettaCore's porphyrin molecular memory (several discrete charge states per molecule in a DRAM-like cell) died before it was integrated into a production flow, partly because molecules had to survive hot back-end steps. Fix: attach the redox-molecule monolayer as the final low-temperature step on finished 180 nm CMOS wafers and read 3-4 discrete oxidation states per cell, giving ~2 bits per cell.
why: Density and charge wall: redox states store charge at fixed potentials, giving more charge per area than a planar capacitor and ~2x bits per cell at an old node.
